title: Atherosclerosis
subtitle: Normal artery → endothelial dysfunction → plaque → rupture → thrombosis

steps.title: Normal artery
steps.text: A healthy artery has a smooth, intact endothelium overlying the intima, a smooth muscle media, and an adventitia. The endothelium releases nitric oxide, keeping the vessel dilated and the surface antithrombotic. Flow is laminar and the lumen is wide.

steps.title: Endothelial dysfunction
steps.text: Disturbed flow at branch points, together with LDL, smoking, hypertension and hyperglycaemia, injures the endothelium. Nitric oxide availability falls, permeability rises, and adhesion molecules appear on the luminal surface.

steps.title: Lipid accumulation
steps.text: ApoB-containing lipoproteins cross the damaged endothelium and are retained by intimal proteoglycans. Once trapped they are oxidatively modified, becoming strongly pro-inflammatory.

steps.title: Foam cell formation
steps.text: Monocytes adhere, migrate into the intima and become macrophages. Scavenger receptors let them ingest modified LDL without normal feedback control, so they become lipid-laden foam cells. Accumulated foam cells form the fatty streak.

steps.title: Plaque development
steps.text: Smooth muscle cells migrate from the media into the intima and secrete collagen, forming a fibrous cap. Dying foam cells release lipid and debris that coalesce into a thrombogenic necrotic core beneath it.

steps.title: Progressive narrowing
steps.text: The artery initially remodels outwards, preserving the lumen despite a growing plaque. Eventually expansion encroaches on the lumen. A stenosis of roughly 70% or more limits flow during exertion and can cause stable angina.

steps.title: Plaque rupture
steps.text: Inflammatory cells release matrix metalloproteinases that thin the fibrous cap while the smooth muscle cells that repair it die. A thin cap over a large necrotic core defines the vulnerable plaque, which fissures and exposes the core to blood.

steps.title: Thrombus formation
steps.text: Platelets adhere to exposed collagen and tissue factor, activate and aggregate, while the coagulation cascade generates a stabilising fibrin mesh. A thrombus forms rapidly on the plaque surface.

steps.title: Reduced blood flow
steps.text: The thrombus critically narrows or occludes the artery. In a coronary artery this produces an acute coronary syndrome; in a cerebral artery, stroke. Crucially, most culprit plaques were not severely stenotic before they ruptured.

title: Myocardial Infarction
subtitle: Normal coronary artery → plaque rupture → thrombosis → obstruction → ischaemia → myocardial injury

steps.title: Normal coronary perfusion
steps.text: The coronary artery supplies its territory of myocardium. Left coronary flow occurs almost entirely in diastole, and myocardial oxygen extraction is already near-maximal at rest, so any increase in demand must be met by increasing flow.

steps.title: Vulnerable plaque
steps.text: A plaque with a thin fibrous cap, a large necrotic core and dense inflammation has developed. It may not be severely stenotic and may never have caused symptoms.

steps.title: Plaque rupture
steps.text: The cap fissures, exposing highly thrombogenic, tissue-factor-rich core material to flowing blood. In plaque erosion the cap remains intact but the endothelium is denuded.

steps.title: Thrombosis
steps.text: Platelets adhere via von Willebrand factor and collagen receptors, activate, release thromboxane A2 and ADP, and aggregate through GPIIb/IIIa receptors. Thrombin generation produces a fibrin mesh that stabilises the growing clot.

steps.title: Vessel obstruction
steps.text: The thrombus, often with accompanying vasospasm, occludes the artery. Complete occlusion typically produces ST elevation; subtotal occlusion produces a non-ST-elevation presentation.

steps.title: Ischaemia
steps.text: Within seconds aerobic metabolism ceases and ATP falls. Contraction stops within about a minute. Anaerobic glycolysis produces lactate, membrane ionic gradients are lost, and the affected wall becomes akinetic.

steps.title: Myocardial injury
steps.text: Irreversible necrosis begins in the subendocardium after roughly 20–30 minutes of complete occlusion and advances as a wavefront towards the epicardium. Cardiac troponin is released into the circulation. This is why time is myocardium.

steps.title: Consequences and healing
steps.text: Loss of contracting myocardium reduces stroke volume and raises filling pressures. Arrhythmia risk peaks early. Over days macrophages clear necrotic tissue — the wall is weakest in the first week — and over weeks collagenous scar forms, with adverse remodelling driving progression towards heart failure.

title: Heart Failure
subtitle: Normal function → myocardial dysfunction → reduced output → compensation → remodelling → progressive dysfunction

steps.title: Normal ventricular function
steps.text: The left ventricle fills at low pressure and ejects roughly 55–70% of its end-diastolic volume. Cardiac output matches metabolic demand, and filling pressures remain normal.

steps.title: Myocardial dysfunction
steps.text: An index injury — infarction, chronic pressure or volume overload, myocarditis, toxin or genetic cardiomyopathy — impairs the heart's ability to eject blood or to fill at normal pressures.

steps.title: Reduced cardiac output
steps.text: Stroke volume falls. Arterial baroreceptors detect reduced arterial filling and reduce their inhibitory signalling to the brainstem cardiovascular centres.

steps.title: Compensatory mechanisms
steps.text: Sympathetic outflow rises, increasing heart rate, contractility and vascular resistance. Reduced renal perfusion activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, causing vasoconstriction and salt and water retention. Blood pressure and perfusion are defended — for now.

steps.title: Congestion
steps.text: Increased preload initially recruits the Frank–Starling mechanism, but the failing ventricle operates on a flattened curve. Further filling raises pressure without raising output, and pressure is transmitted back to the lungs and systemic veins.

steps.title: Ventricular remodelling
steps.text: Chronic neurohormonal stimulation and mechanical stress cause myocyte hypertrophy, apoptosis and interstitial fibrosis. The ventricle dilates and becomes more spherical, which by Laplace's law increases wall stress and worsens efficiency.

steps.title: Secondary valve dysfunction
steps.text: Annular dilatation and papillary muscle displacement produce functional mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, adding a volume load to an already failing ventricle.

steps.title: Progressive dysfunction
steps.text: Remodelling begets further dysfunction in a self-reinforcing cycle, punctuated by decompensations. Interrupting the neurohormonal limb of this cycle is precisely what guideline-directed medical therapy does — and why it prolongs life.

title: Aortic Stenosis
subtitle: Normal valve → leaflet thickening and calcification → reduced opening → pressure gradient → ventricular adaptation → clinical consequences

steps.title: Normal aortic valve
steps.text: Three thin, pliable semilunar cusps open widely in systole, giving an orifice area of roughly 3–4 cm² and essentially no pressure gradient between the left ventricle and the aorta.

steps.title: Leaflet injury and lipid entry
steps.text: Mechanical stress, greatest on the aortic side of the cusps, damages the valvular endothelium. Lipoproteins enter the leaflet and are oxidatively modified, initiating a chronic inflammatory response.

steps.title: Calcification
steps.text: Valvular interstitial cells adopt an osteoblast-like phenotype and deposit calcium hydroxyapatite within the leaflet. This is an active, regulated biology — not simple wear and tear. A bicuspid valve undergoes the same process one to two decades earlier.

steps.title: Reduced opening
steps.text: Progressive calcification stiffens the cusps and restricts their excursion. Unlike rheumatic disease, degenerative calcific stenosis characteristically spares the commissures.

steps.title: Rising pressure gradient
steps.text: As the effective orifice falls, a systolic gradient develops between ventricle and aorta and transvalvular velocity rises. Severe stenosis is defined by an area under 1.0 cm², a mean gradient of 40 mmHg or more, or a peak velocity of 4 m/s or more.

steps.title: Ventricular adaptation
steps.text: By Laplace's law, the ventricle adds sarcomeres in parallel to normalise wall stress. Concentric hypertrophy preserves ejection fraction and stroke volume for years — this is the long compensated, asymptomatic phase.

steps.title: Ischaemia and diastolic dysfunction
steps.text: The hypertrophied ventricle relaxes poorly, raising filling pressures. Increased muscle mass raises oxygen demand while raised end-diastolic pressure and shortened diastole reduce coronary perfusion. Angina occurs even with normal coronary arteries.

steps.title: Clinical consequences
steps.text: Angina, exertional syncope from a fixed stroke volume, and heart failure appear. Once symptoms develop, survival without intervention falls sharply — which is why symptom onset is the trigger for valve replacement.

title: Atrial Fibrillation
subtitle: Normal atrial activation → ectopic triggers → chaotic activity → loss of atrial contraction → irregular ventricular response

steps.title: Normal atrial activation
steps.text: The sinuatrial node depolarises spontaneously and the impulse spreads as an organised wavefront across both atria, producing a P wave and a coordinated atrial contraction that completes ventricular filling.

steps.title: Substrate development
steps.text: Atrial stretch, fibrosis, inflammation and ageing make conduction slow and heterogeneous, and shorten and disperse refractory periods. This is the substrate on which fibrillation can be sustained.

steps.title: Ectopic triggers
steps.text: Rapidly firing foci within the myocardial sleeves of the pulmonary veins generate premature atrial beats. This observation is what made pulmonary vein isolation the cornerstone of ablation.

steps.title: Chaotic electrical activity
steps.text: Multiple simultaneous re-entrant wavelets and rotors propagate through the atria in continually changing directions, at atrial rates of roughly 300–600 per minute. The organised P wave is replaced by a fibrillatory baseline.

steps.title: Loss of atrial contraction
steps.text: Because activation is disorganised, the atria never contract as a unit. The atrial kick is lost, reducing ventricular filling by up to 20–30% — a loss that matters most when the ventricle is stiff.

steps.title: Irregular ventricular response
steps.text: The AV node conducts some impulses and blocks others through decremental and concealed conduction, producing the irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm — typically 100–160 per minute if untreated.

steps.title: Stasis and thrombus
steps.text: Blood stagnates in the non-contracting atrium, particularly in the trabeculated left atrial appendage. Combined with endothelial dysfunction and a prothrombotic state, this promotes thrombus formation.

steps.title: Embolism and remodelling
steps.text: Thrombus may embolise and cause ischaemic stroke — the reason anticoagulation decisions rest on stroke risk rather than symptoms. Meanwhile fibrillation itself promotes further remodelling: atrial fibrillation begets atrial fibrillation.

title: Aortic Aneurysm
subtitle: Medial degeneration → dilatation → Laplace amplification → mural thrombus → rupture

steps.title: Normal aorta
steps.text: The aortic wall has three layers. Elastic lamellae in the media store energy in systole and recoil in diastole, so the wall tolerates a lifetime of pulsatile stress at a stable calibre.

steps.title: Medial degeneration
steps.text: Elastin fragmentation, smooth muscle cell loss and proteoglycan accumulation weaken the media — the common final pathway whatever the initiating cause, whether atherosclerotic, inflammatory or genetic.

steps.title: Proteolytic activity
steps.text: Matrix metalloproteinases released by infiltrating inflammatory cells degrade elastin and collagen faster than they can be replaced, so each cardiac cycle leaves the wall a little weaker.

steps.title: Loss of wall strength
steps.text: The weakened segment yields to arterial pressure and begins to dilate. Dilatation is initially slow and entirely silent, which is why aneurysms are usually found incidentally or by screening.

steps.title: Laplace's law amplification
steps.text: Wall tension is proportional to pressure multiplied by radius. Every increment of dilatation raises tension, which accelerates further dilatation — an inherently self-accelerating process, and the reason expansion rate rises with size.

steps.title: Mural thrombus
steps.text: Flow within the sac becomes recirculating and slow, and laminated thrombus forms along the wall. It may embolise distally, and it impairs oxygen diffusion to the already ischaemic outer media.

steps.title: Rupture
steps.text: When wall stress exceeds tensile strength the wall tears. Free rupture into the peritoneum is usually rapidly fatal; a contained retroperitoneal rupture may allow just enough time for emergency repair.

title: Aortic Dissection
subtitle: Intimal tear → false lumen → branch malperfusion → proximal complications → rupture

steps.title: Medial vulnerability
steps.text: Cystic medial degeneration, long-standing hypertensive injury or a genetic connective tissue defect weakens the media and reduces its resistance to the shear generated by each pulse.

steps.title: Intimal tear
steps.text: A tear opens, most often in the ascending aorta just above the sinotubular junction or just distal to the left subclavian artery — the two points of greatest hydrodynamic stress.

steps.title: False lumen propagation
steps.text: Blood driven by systolic pressure, and above all by the rate of pressure rise (dP/dt), enters the media and dissects along it — usually antegrade, sometimes retrograde. This is why treatment targets heart rate before pressure.

steps.title: Branch vessel compromise
steps.text: The dissection flap can cover branch origins and cause malperfusion: stroke from carotid involvement, infarction from coronary involvement (classically the right), paraplegia, renal failure, mesenteric or limb ischaemia.

steps.title: Proximal complications
steps.text: Retrograde extension into the root disrupts cusp support and causes acute aortic regurgitation, may rupture into the pericardium causing tamponade, or may occlude a coronary ostium.

steps.title: External rupture
steps.text: Rupture through the adventitia into the pericardium, pleural space or mediastinum causes rapid haemodynamic collapse — the usual mechanism of death, and the reason mortality climbs with every hour of delay.

title: Pulmonary Embolism
subtitle: Venous thrombus → embolisation → raised pulmonary resistance → right ventricular failure → obstructive shock

steps.title: Thrombus formation
steps.text: Virchow's triad — venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability — promotes thrombus formation, most often in the deep veins of the calf and thigh.

steps.title: Embolisation
steps.text: Thrombus detaches and travels through the venous system, right atrium and right ventricle into the pulmonary arteries, lodging where the vessel calibre narrows.

steps.title: Pulmonary vascular resistance rises
steps.text: Mechanical obstruction is compounded by hypoxic vasoconstriction and by vasoactive mediators such as serotonin and thromboxane released from activated platelets, so resistance rises more than the clot burden alone would predict.

steps.title: Right ventricular strain
steps.text: The thin-walled right ventricle is exquisitely afterload-sensitive. Acute pressure loading dilates it, raises wall tension and reduces right coronary perfusion, and the ventricle can fail abruptly.

steps.title: Ventricular interdependence
steps.text: Within the fixed pericardium the dilated right ventricle displaces the interventricular septum leftwards, impairing left ventricular filling and reducing cardiac output — the D-shaped septum seen on echocardiography.

steps.title: Gas exchange abnormality
steps.text: Perfused-but-not-ventilated and ventilated-but-not-perfused regions coexist. Dead space rises, shunt and V/Q mismatch cause hypoxaemia, and tachypnoea produces a respiratory alkalosis.

steps.title: Pulmonary infarction
steps.text: The lung's dual blood supply makes infarction uncommon; it occurs mainly with distal emboli or coexisting cardiopulmonary disease, and then causes pleuritic pain and haemoptysis.

steps.title: Obstructive shock
steps.text: With massive embolism right ventricular output collapses, left ventricular preload falls, and systemic hypotension and cardiac arrest follow — often as pulseless electrical activity.

title: Deep Vein Thrombosis
subtitle: Valve-pocket nidus → propagation → obstruction → embolisation → post-thrombotic syndrome

steps.title: Virchow's triad
steps.text: Stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability combine to tip the balance towards thrombosis. Most clinical situations — surgery, immobility, malignancy, pregnancy — involve at least two of the three.

steps.title: Initiation in valve pockets
steps.text: Thrombi typically begin in the low-flow, relatively hypoxic pockets behind venous valves, most often in the calf veins, where local hypoxia activates the endothelium.

steps.title: Propagation
steps.text: Fibrin and trapped red cells extend the thrombus along the vein. Proximal extension above the knee substantially increases the risk of a clinically significant embolism.

steps.title: Inflammation and obstruction
steps.text: The thrombus provokes inflammation in the vein wall, producing pain, warmth and tenderness, while obstruction raises distal venous pressure and causes unilateral swelling.

steps.title: Embolisation
steps.text: Fragments detach and travel through the right heart to the pulmonary circulation. Proximal thrombus carries far greater risk than isolated distal calf thrombus.

steps.title: Resolution and recanalisation
steps.text: Fibrinolysis and organisation partly clear the thrombus over weeks to months and a channel reopens, but the valve leaflets are frequently damaged in the process.

steps.title: Post-thrombotic syndrome
steps.text: Residual obstruction and valvular incompetence cause chronic ambulatory venous hypertension, producing pain, swelling, skin changes and sometimes ulceration in a substantial minority of patients.

title: Pulmonary Hypertension
subtitle: Vascular injury → remodelling → rising resistance → right ventricular adaptation and decompensation

steps.title: Initiating insult
steps.text: Depending on the group: pulmonary arterial endothelial injury, sustained backward transmission of raised left atrial pressure, chronic alveolar hypoxia, or unresolved thromboembolic obstruction.

steps.title: Vasoconstriction
steps.text: Reduced nitric oxide and prostacyclin with increased endothelin-1 produce sustained vasoconstriction — the three pathways targeted by modern group 1 therapies.

steps.title: Vascular remodelling
steps.text: Intimal proliferation, medial hypertrophy and adventitial fibrosis progressively narrow the small pulmonary arteries, and plexiform lesions appear in advanced group 1 disease.

steps.title: In situ thrombosis
steps.text: Endothelial dysfunction and sluggish flow promote thrombosis within small vessels, obliterating further cross-sectional area.

steps.title: Rising pulmonary vascular resistance
steps.text: The pulmonary bed normally has enormous recruitment reserve, so pressure rises appreciably only once a large proportion of the vasculature is lost — which is why presentation is late and often advanced.

steps.title: Right ventricular adaptation
steps.text: The right ventricle hypertrophies to meet the load. This adaptive, concentric phase can be maintained for years with relatively preserved function and few symptoms.

steps.title: Right ventricular decompensation
steps.text: Eventually the ventricle dilates and becomes spherical. Rising wall tension reduces right coronary perfusion, and functional tricuspid regurgitation develops, volume-loading an already failing chamber.

steps.title: Interdependence and low output
steps.text: The dilated right ventricle shifts the septum leftwards and impairs left ventricular filling. Cardiac output falls, producing exertional syncope and, ultimately, right heart failure and death.

title: Hypertension
subtitle: Resistance and sodium handling → remodelling → arterial stiffening → hypertensive heart disease

steps.title: Determinants of pressure
steps.text: Mean arterial pressure is the product of cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance. In established primary hypertension the dominant abnormality is raised resistance with a normal cardiac output.

steps.title: Sodium and volume handling
steps.text: A rightward shift in the renal pressure–natriuresis relationship means the kidney needs a higher perfusion pressure to excrete a given sodium load, resetting arterial pressure upward.

steps.title: Neurohormonal activation
steps.text: Increased sympathetic outflow and inappropriate activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system raise vascular tone and promote sodium retention and vascular growth.

steps.title: Endothelial dysfunction
steps.text: Reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, with increased endothelin and oxidative stress, shifts the vascular balance towards vasoconstriction and away from repair.

steps.title: Vascular remodelling
steps.text: Resistance arterioles undergo hypertrophic and eutrophic remodelling with an increased wall-to-lumen ratio. Because resistance varies with the fourth power of the radius, small changes raise pressure sharply — and the cycle perpetuates itself.

steps.title: Large artery stiffening
steps.text: Elastin fragmentation and collagen deposition reduce aortic compliance. Pulse waves return earlier and augment the systolic peak, raising systolic and pulse pressure — the mechanism of isolated systolic hypertension in older people.

steps.title: Cardiac consequences
steps.text: Chronic pressure loading produces concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with impaired relaxation and reduced coronary flow reserve, atrial dilatation, and a rising risk of atrial fibrillation, heart failure and stroke.

title: Peripheral Arterial Disease
subtitle: Limb atherosclerosis → claudication → rest pain → tissue loss → acute limb ischaemia

steps.title: Atherosclerotic plaque formation
steps.text: The same lipid-driven inflammatory process seen in the coronary arteries develops in the aortoiliac, femoropopliteal and infrapopliteal segments — which is why peripheral disease predicts coronary and cerebrovascular events.

steps.title: Progressive stenosis
steps.text: Resting flow is preserved for a long time because the distal bed vasodilates and collateral channels enlarge around the obstruction.

steps.title: Exercise-induced ischaemia
steps.text: Walking raises muscular demand above the maximum deliverable flow. Anaerobic metabolism and metabolite accumulation produce the cramping pain of claudication, reproducible at a given distance and relieved by rest within minutes.

steps.title: Falling ankle pressure
steps.text: The pressure drop across the lesion is measurable at the ankle. A resting ankle–brachial index below 0.9 confirms disease; below 0.4 indicates severe ischaemia.

steps.title: Progression to rest pain
steps.text: When obstruction is severe enough that even resting metabolic demand cannot be met, ischaemic rest pain occurs — classically in the forefoot, worse lying flat and relieved by hanging the leg over the edge of the bed.

steps.title: Tissue loss
steps.text: Critically reduced perfusion prevents healing of minor trauma, producing ulceration and then gangrene. In diabetes, neuropathy masks the pain and infection accelerates tissue loss.

steps.title: Acute limb ischaemia
steps.text: Sudden occlusion — thrombosis of a diseased segment, or embolism — produces the six Ps and threatens the limb within hours, leaving no time for collaterals to develop.

title: Chronic Venous Insufficiency
subtitle: Valve failure → ambulatory venous hypertension → skin change → venous ulceration

steps.title: The normal calf pump
steps.text: Calf contraction empties the deep veins and competent valves prevent backflow, so venous pressure at the ankle falls markedly on walking and the capillary bed is protected.

steps.title: Valve incompetence
steps.text: Vein wall weakness and dilatation separate the valve cusps so they no longer meet, allowing blood to reflux down the vein under gravity.

steps.title: Loss of the pump advantage
steps.text: With incompetent valves each contraction is followed by rapid refilling from above, so ambulatory venous pressure fails to fall — the haemodynamic hallmark of the disease.

steps.title: Sustained venous hypertension
steps.text: Persistently high venous pressure is transmitted to the capillary bed, raising capillary hydrostatic pressure throughout standing and walking.

steps.title: Capillary leakage and inflammation
steps.text: Fluid, proteins and red cells extravasate. Haemoglobin breakdown deposits haemosiderin, producing the characteristic brown staining, while trapped and activated leucocytes sustain inflammation.

steps.title: Fibrosis and skin change
steps.text: Chronic inflammation causes dermal fibrosis and subcutaneous induration — lipodermatosclerosis — producing the inverted champagne bottle contour of the lower leg.

steps.title: Ulceration
steps.text: Impaired microcirculation and nutrient exchange leave the skin unable to heal minor trauma, producing shallow, exudative ulcers in the gaiter area — treated by compression, which restores the pressure gradient.

title: Aortic Regurgitation
subtitle: Loss of coaptation → volume overload → eccentric hypertrophy → wide pulse pressure → decompensation

steps.title: Competent valve
steps.text: In diastole the three cusps meet along their coaptation surfaces and the column of aortic blood holds them shut, so the ventricle fills only across the mitral valve.

steps.title: Loss of cusp coaptation
steps.text: Cusp disease — bicuspid, rheumatic, endocarditic — or dilatation of the annulus and root pulls the cusps apart, so they no longer seal and blood flows back into the ventricle throughout diastole.

steps.title: Volume overload
steps.text: The ventricle receives its normal transmitral filling plus the regurgitant volume, so end-diastolic volume rises substantially and total stroke volume must rise to match.

steps.title: Eccentric hypertrophy
steps.text: In chronic disease the ventricle adds sarcomeres in series, dilating while remaining relatively compliant. It can accommodate a large volume at acceptable filling pressures — which is why chronic disease is tolerated for years.

steps.title: Combined pressure load
steps.text: Ejecting a large total stroke volume raises systolic pressure, so the ventricle faces volume loading and pressure loading together — a uniquely demanding combination.

steps.title: Wide pulse pressure
steps.text: High systolic pressure with a low aortic diastolic pressure produces the wide pulse pressure, the collapsing pulse and the many named peripheral signs of chronic aortic regurgitation.

steps.title: Coronary compromise
steps.text: Coronary perfusion depends on aortic diastolic pressure, which is now low, while hypertrophy raises demand — so angina can occur with entirely normal coronary arteries.

steps.title: Decompensation
steps.text: Progressive dilatation eventually outstrips compensation. Contractility falls, ejection fraction declines and symptoms appear — often after irreversible myocardial change has begun, which is why surveillance triggers surgery before symptoms.

title: Mitral Stenosis
subtitle: Rheumatic valvulitis → commissural fusion → transmitral gradient → pulmonary congestion → right heart failure

steps.title: Rheumatic valvulitis
steps.text: Molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein and cardiac tissue provokes an immune response that damages the valve, often decades before any symptom appears.

steps.title: Commissural fusion
steps.text: Chronic inflammation fuses the commissures, thickens and calcifies the leaflets and shortens the chordae, converting the funnel-shaped valve into a rigid fish-mouth orifice.

steps.title: Transmitral gradient
steps.text: A diastolic pressure gradient develops between the left atrium and ventricle. Because it depends on flow and on diastolic filling time, tachycardia — exercise, fever, pregnancy — sharply worsens it.

steps.title: Left atrial hypertension
steps.text: Raised atrial pressure dilates the chamber and, transmitted backwards through valveless pulmonary veins, raises pulmonary capillary pressure and causes exertional breathlessness and orthopnoea.

steps.title: Pulmonary vascular change
steps.text: Sustained pulmonary venous hypertension causes reactive arteriolar vasoconstriction and eventually fixed remodelling, producing pulmonary hypertension on top of the venous congestion.

steps.title: Right heart consequences
steps.text: Right ventricular pressure overload leads to hypertrophy, then dilatation, functional tricuspid regurgitation and the signs of right heart failure.

steps.title: Atrial fibrillation and embolism
steps.text: Atrial dilatation and fibrosis promote atrial fibrillation, which removes the atrial contribution to filling at the very moment it is most needed and greatly raises the risk of left atrial thrombus and systemic embolism.

title: Mitral Regurgitation
subtitle: Loss of coaptation → regurgitant volume → biatrial and ventricular overload → the vicious cycle

steps.title: Loss of coaptation
steps.text: Either the leaflets themselves are abnormal — prolapse, flail, rheumatic or infective disease — or the apparatus is geometrically distorted by ventricular dilatation, so the valve cannot seal in systole.

steps.title: Regurgitant volume
steps.text: Part of the stroke volume is ejected backwards into the low-pressure left atrium. Because the ventricle empties partly into a low-impedance chamber it is unloaded, so ejection fraction looks deceptively good.

steps.title: Left atrial volume overload
steps.text: The atrium receives pulmonary venous return plus the regurgitant volume. In chronic disease it dilates and stays compliant, so pressure rises only modestly and symptoms are late.

steps.title: Left ventricular volume overload
steps.text: The whole regurgitant volume returns across the mitral valve in diastole, so the ventricle handles it twice over — producing eccentric hypertrophy and progressive dilatation.

steps.title: The vicious cycle
steps.text: In secondary regurgitation, ventricular dilatation tethers the leaflets and worsens the leak, which further volume-loads and dilates the ventricle — regurgitation begetting regurgitation.

steps.title: Progressive myocardial dysfunction
steps.text: Chronic volume overload eventually impairs contractility. Because the ventricle has been chronically unloaded, an apparently normal ejection fraction may already represent significant dysfunction — hence the lower operative thresholds used in this lesion.

steps.title: Acute regurgitation
steps.text: With sudden severe regurgitation — chordal rupture, papillary muscle rupture, endocarditis — the small non-compliant atrium cannot accommodate the volume. Atrial and pulmonary venous pressures rise abruptly, causing flash pulmonary oedema and shock.

title: Tricuspid Regurgitation
subtitle: Right ventricular remodelling → annular dilatation and tethering → systemic venous congestion

steps.title: Right ventricular overload
steps.text: Left heart disease, pulmonary hypertension or intrinsic right ventricular disease loads the thin-walled right ventricle with pressure or volume, and it dilates.

steps.title: Annular dilatation
steps.text: The non-planar tricuspid annulus dilates, predominantly along its free wall where there is no fibrous support, increasing the distance the leaflets must cover to meet.

steps.title: Leaflet tethering
steps.text: As the ventricle remodels, the papillary muscles are displaced apically and outwards, tethering the leaflets away from the annular plane and further reducing coaptation.

steps.title: Regurgitant volume and atrial overload
steps.text: Systolic backflow raises right atrial pressure, producing a giant v wave, and transmits that pressure directly into the systemic veins — visible as a raised, pulsatile jugular venous pulse.

steps.title: The self-perpetuating cycle
steps.text: Volume overload dilates the right ventricle further, which worsens annular dilatation and tethering — regurgitation begetting regurgitation, independent of the original cause.

steps.title: Systemic venous congestion
steps.text: Sustained venous hypertension produces hepatic congestion with a pulsatile liver, ascites and peripheral oedema, and eventually cardiac cirrhosis and cardiorenal dysfunction — the reason severe tricuspid regurgitation carries an independent prognostic penalty.

title: Infective Endocarditis
subtitle: Endothelial injury → sterile nidus → bacterial adherence → vegetation → destruction and embolism

steps.title: Endothelial injury
steps.text: Turbulent flow across an abnormal valve, the jet lesion where a regurgitant stream strikes endocardium, or direct trauma from a catheter or pacing lead damages the endocardial surface.

steps.title: Sterile vegetation
steps.text: Platelets and fibrin deposit at the site of injury, forming non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis — the nidus that circulating organisms can colonise.

steps.title: Bacteraemia and adherence
steps.text: Organisms entering the bloodstream from the mouth, skin, gut or an indwelling line adhere to the thrombus using surface adhesins. Staphylococcus aureus can also stick to intact endothelium, which is why it infects normal valves.

steps.title: Vegetation growth
steps.text: Bacteria proliferate and are progressively encased in fibrin and platelets, sheltered from neutrophils and reaching very high local density — which is why treatment must be prolonged, bactericidal and parenteral.

steps.title: Local destruction
steps.text: Infection erodes the leaflets, causing perforation and chordal rupture with acute regurgitation, and may burrow into surrounding tissue to form abscesses, pseudoaneurysms and fistulae.

steps.title: Conduction involvement
steps.text: An aortic root abscess extending towards the membranous septum can interrupt the bundle of His, so a new conduction abnormality on the ECG is an important warning of perivalvular extension.

steps.title: Systemic embolisation
steps.text: Fragments of vegetation embolise — to brain, spleen, kidneys and limbs from left-sided disease, and to the lungs from right-sided disease — causing infarction, abscess and mycotic aneurysm.

steps.title: Immune phenomena
steps.text: Circulating immune complexes deposit in tissues, producing glomerulonephritis, Osler's nodes and Roth spots — the immunological half of the modified Duke criteria.

title: Rheumatic Heart Disease
subtitle: Streptococcal pharyngitis → molecular mimicry → acute carditis → chronic valve scarring

steps.title: Streptococcal pharyngitis
steps.text: Infection of the throat with group A Streptococcus pyogenes, particularly rheumatogenic M-protein strains, in a genetically susceptible host — the single preventable step in the whole sequence.

steps.title: Molecular mimicry
steps.text: Antibodies and T cells raised against streptococcal M protein and group A carbohydrate cross-react with human proteins including cardiac myosin and valvular laminin.

steps.title: Acute rheumatic fever
steps.text: Two to four weeks later a multisystem illness develops — carditis, migratory polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules — recognised using the revised Jones criteria.

steps.title: Acute carditis
steps.text: Pancarditis affects endocardium, myocardium and pericardium. Verrucous vegetations form along the leaflet closure lines, and the valve — most often the mitral — leaks.

steps.title: Aschoff bodies
steps.text: Granulomatous lesions containing Anitschkow cells appear in the myocardium — the histological signature of rheumatic carditis, and evidence that the myocardium is involved as well as the valve.

steps.title: Chronic scarring
steps.text: Over years, healing produces commissural fusion, leaflet thickening and calcification, and chordal shortening and fusion — converting the acute regurgitation into predominant stenosis.

steps.title: Effect of recurrence
steps.text: Each further episode of acute rheumatic fever adds damage, so the cumulative burden depends heavily on whether recurrences are prevented — which is what secondary prophylaxis with penicillin achieves.

title: Stable Angina
subtitle: Fixed stenosis → exhausted flow reserve → supply–demand mismatch → the ischaemic cascade

steps.title: Fixed stenosis develops
steps.text: An atherosclerotic plaque progressively narrows an epicardial artery. Resting flow is maintained because the distal microvasculature dilates to compensate.

steps.title: Coronary flow reserve falls
steps.text: Because the microvasculature is already partly dilated just to keep resting flow normal, the capacity for further dilatation — the coronary flow reserve — is reduced.

steps.title: Demand rises with exertion
steps.text: Exercise raises heart rate, contractility and wall stress, and therefore myocardial oxygen demand. Tachycardia simultaneously shortens diastole, which is when the left ventricle is actually perfused.

steps.title: Supply–demand mismatch
steps.text: When demand exceeds the maximum achievable supply, the subendocardium — perfused last and compressed most — becomes ischaemic first.

steps.title: The ischaemic cascade
steps.text: Anaerobic metabolism, lactate production and adenosine release stimulate cardiac afferents. Regional diastolic then systolic dysfunction appears, followed by ECG change and only finally by pain — which is why silent ischaemia exists.

steps.title: Resolution
steps.text: Stopping lowers demand, flow again becomes adequate and everything reverses within minutes. No myocyte necrosis occurs and troponin stays normal — the defining difference from an acute coronary syndrome.

title: Cardiomyopathies
subtitle: Dilated · hypertrophic · restrictive · arrhythmogenic — four phenotypes, shared endpoints

steps.title: The normal ventricle
steps.text: A normal left ventricle has a wall of roughly 10 mm, an ellipsoidal cavity, brisk contraction and unimpeded early filling. Each cardiomyopathy departs from this reference in a characteristic direction.

steps.title: Dilated cardiomyopathy
steps.text: Myocyte injury, loss and disarray with interstitial fibrosis lead to eccentric remodelling. The ventricle dilates and becomes spherical, wall stress rises by Laplace's law and systolic function progressively declines.

steps.title: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
steps.text: Sarcomeric protein mutations produce myocyte hypertrophy and disarray with interstitial fibrosis. Wall thickening is typically asymmetric and septal, impairing relaxation and reducing cavity size.

steps.title: Dynamic outflow obstruction
steps.text: In the obstructive form, septal hypertrophy narrows the outflow tract and rapid flow drags the anterior mitral leaflet into it — systolic anterior motion — causing dynamic obstruction and mitral regurgitation. The gradient rises when preload falls or contractility increases.

steps.title: Restrictive cardiomyopathy
steps.text: Infiltration or fibrosis stiffens the myocardium. Volumes and systolic function are initially preserved but filling is severely impaired, producing marked biatrial dilatation and high filling pressures.

steps.title: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy
steps.text: Desmosomal mutations weaken cell-to-cell adhesion. Myocytes are progressively replaced by fibrous and fatty tissue, mostly in the right ventricle, creating a substrate for re-entrant ventricular arrhythmia that exercise makes worse.

steps.title: Shared consequences
steps.text: Whatever the mechanism, the endpoints converge: heart failure, arrhythmia and thromboembolism — with sudden cardiac death a particular concern in the hypertrophic and arrhythmogenic forms, and a family screening obligation in all of them.

title: Congenital Heart Disease
subtitle: Embryological lesion → transitional circulation → shunt, obstruction or cyanosis → Eisenmenger

steps.title: Disrupted development
steps.text: Abnormal septation, valve formation, outflow tract division or conotruncal rotation between roughly weeks three and eight of gestation produces the structural lesion.

steps.title: Transitional circulation
steps.text: At birth pulmonary vascular resistance falls and systemic resistance rises. That reversal is what unmasks many left-to-right shunts, so lesions may present weeks after birth rather than immediately.

steps.title: Left-to-right shunting
steps.text: A communication between the circuits directs blood towards the lower-resistance pulmonary side, causing pulmonary overcirculation and volume loading of the receiving chambers.

steps.title: Obstructive physiology
steps.text: Stenotic lesions — pulmonary stenosis, aortic stenosis, coarctation — impose pressure loading instead, producing hypertrophy and, if severe, ventricular failure.

steps.title: Cyanotic physiology
steps.text: Right-to-left shunting or abnormal mixing delivers deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation, producing hypoxaemia, secondary erythrocytosis and clubbing.

steps.title: Eisenmenger physiology
steps.text: Long-standing high-flow shunting remodels the pulmonary vasculature until resistance exceeds systemic and the shunt reverses. Cyanosis appears, and closure of the defect is then no longer possible — which is why timing of repair matters so much.

title: Atrial Septal Defect
subtitle: Compliance-driven shunt → right heart volume overload → fixed splitting → late arrhythmia

steps.title: The defect
steps.text: A persistent communication in the interatrial septum — most often a secundum defect at the fossa ovalis — allows blood to cross between the atria.

steps.title: Compliance-driven shunting
steps.text: The right ventricle is more compliant than the left, so in diastole the left atrium preferentially empties across the defect. The shunt is determined by relative ventricular compliance, not by a pressure difference between the atria.

steps.title: Right heart volume overload
steps.text: The right atrium and ventricle receive normal systemic venous return plus the shunted volume, and progressively dilate. The left heart, by contrast, stays normal or small.

steps.title: Increased pulmonary blood flow
steps.text: Pulmonary flow may be one and a half to three times systemic flow. That extra flow across structurally normal pulmonary and tricuspid valves produces the characteristic flow murmurs.

steps.title: Fixed splitting of S2
steps.text: The large, relatively fixed right ventricular volume load prolongs right ventricular ejection throughout the respiratory cycle, so the normal inspiratory widening of the split disappears — the classic auscultatory sign.

steps.title: Atrial remodelling and arrhythmia
steps.text: Chronic right atrial dilatation and stretch remodel the atrial myocardium, producing atrial fibrillation and flutter, typically from the fourth decade onwards.

steps.title: Pulmonary vascular disease
steps.text: In a minority, sustained high pulmonary flow causes vascular remodelling and rising resistance, eventually reversing the shunt — Eisenmenger syndrome — after which closure is no longer possible.

title: Pericardial Disease
subtitle: Pericarditis → effusion → tamponade physiology → constriction

steps.title: Pericardial inflammation
steps.text: An infectious, autoimmune, metabolic or traumatic insult inflames the pericardial layers. The roughened surfaces rub together, producing a friction rub and sharp pleuritic pain that eases on sitting forward.

steps.title: Pain referral
steps.text: Inflammation irritating the adjacent diaphragmatic pleura stimulates the phrenic nerve, referring pain to the trapezius ridge — a highly specific feature of pericarditis.

steps.title: Effusion formation
steps.text: Inflammation increases capillary permeability and fluid exudes into the pericardial space. A slowly accumulating effusion can become very large without any haemodynamic effect.

steps.title: Rising intrapericardial pressure
steps.text: The parietal pericardium is relatively non-compliant in the short term. Once the pericardial reserve volume is used up, each further millilitre causes a steep rise in intrapericardial pressure.

steps.title: Tamponade physiology
steps.text: Raised pressure compresses the thin-walled right-sided chambers and limits diastolic filling. Filling pressures equalise across the chambers, stroke volume falls, and tachycardia and vasoconstriction hold blood pressure up until sudden decompensation.

steps.title: Enhanced interdependence
steps.text: With total cardiac volume fixed by the sac, the inspiratory increase in right ventricular filling pushes the septum leftwards and reduces left ventricular filling — producing pulsus paradoxus.

steps.title: Constriction
steps.text: Chronic inflammation leaves the pericardium fibrotic, thickened and sometimes calcified. Early diastolic filling is rapid and unimpeded but stops abruptly at the pericardial limit, producing the dip-and-plateau waveform and a pericardial knock.

title: Supraventricular Tachycardia
subtitle: Dual pathways → premature beat → re-entry → rapid regular tachycardia

steps.title: Dual pathway physiology
steps.text: In AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia the AV nodal region has two functionally distinct routes: a fast pathway that conducts quickly but recovers slowly, and a slow pathway that conducts slowly but recovers quickly.

steps.title: Normal sinus conduction
steps.text: In sinus rhythm the impulse travels down both pathways. The fast pathway arrives first, activates the ventricle and collides retrogradely with the slow-pathway wavefront, extinguishing it.

steps.title: Initiation by a premature beat
steps.text: A premature atrial beat arrives while the fast pathway is still refractory, so it can only conduct down the slow pathway — seen on the ECG as a sudden jump in the PR interval.

steps.title: Re-entry established
steps.text: By the time the impulse reaches the distal node the fast pathway has recovered and conducts it retrogradely to the atrium, completing a circuit that then perpetuates itself beat after beat.

steps.title: The tachycardia
steps.text: The circuit drives the ventricles at 150–250 per minute. Atria and ventricles activate almost simultaneously, so the retrograde P wave is buried in or just after the QRS — the pseudo-R′ in V1.

steps.title: Accessory pathway variant
steps.text: In AV re-entrant tachycardia the circuit uses the AV node in one direction and an accessory pathway in the other. Orthodromic conduction gives a narrow QRS; antidromic conduction gives a wide one.

steps.title: Haemodynamic effect
steps.text: Rapid rates shorten diastolic filling and reduce stroke volume. Atria contracting against closed AV valves produce cannon a waves and the sensation of pounding in the neck.

steps.title: Danger in pre-excited AF
steps.text: If atrial fibrillation occurs with an accessory pathway that lacks the AV node's decremental properties, conduction can be extremely rapid and irregular, and may degenerate into ventricular fibrillation — the reason AV nodal blockers are avoided here.

title: Ventricular Arrhythmias
subtitle: Scar, triggers and channelopathy → ventricular tachycardia → fibrillation → arrest

steps.title: Scar-related re-entry
steps.text: Surviving myocyte bundles threading through infarct scar conduct slowly and anisotropically. They form a protected isthmus around which a fixed circuit can turn, sustaining monomorphic ventricular tachycardia.

steps.title: Triggered activity
steps.text: Early afterdepolarisations during a prolonged repolarisation phase can trigger torsades de pointes; delayed afterdepolarisations from calcium overload underlie catecholaminergic arrhythmias.

steps.title: Abnormal automaticity
steps.text: Ischaemic or injured Purkinje and ventricular tissue can develop enhanced spontaneous depolarisation and take over as an ectopic focus, generating ventricular ectopy and accelerated idioventricular rhythms.

steps.title: Channelopathy substrate
steps.text: Inherited abnormalities of sodium, potassium or calcium handling alter action potential duration and increase dispersion of repolarisation, creating vulnerability in a structurally normal heart.

steps.title: Haemodynamic collapse
steps.text: Even organised ventricular tachycardia at a rapid rate severely limits filling. With impaired ventricular function it quickly causes hypotension, syncope and loss of consciousness.

steps.title: Degeneration to fibrillation
steps.text: Wavebreak fragments the organised circuit into multiple wandering wavelets. The ventricles quiver without ejecting, cardiac output ceases, and death follows within minutes unless defibrillation restores organised activation.

title: Conduction Disorders & Bradyarrhythmias
subtitle: Conduction system disease → Wenckebach → complete block → escape dependence

steps.title: The normal conduction system
steps.text: The sinus node sets the rate; the AV node delays the impulse to allow atrial contribution to filling; the His–Purkinje system then activates both ventricles almost simultaneously, giving a narrow QRS.

steps.title: Age-related degeneration
steps.text: Progressive fibrosis and calcification of the conduction system — historically Lev's and Lenègre's disease — is the commonest cause of acquired block in older adults.

steps.title: Ischaemic injury
steps.text: Inferior infarction may cause nodal block through AV nodal artery involvement or vagal tone, and is usually transient. Block complicating anterior infarction implies extensive septal necrosis and carries a far worse prognosis.

steps.title: Nodal versus infranodal block
steps.text: Block within the AV node produces a narrow-complex escape at 40–60 per minute that often improves with atropine. Infranodal block leaves a slow, unreliable wide-complex escape at 20–40 per minute that does not.

steps.title: Wenckebach physiology
steps.text: In Mobitz type I block, progressive fatigue of nodal conduction lengthens the PR interval beat by beat until one impulse fails entirely. The node then recovers and the cycle repeats — the grouped beating seen on the strip.

steps.title: Escape rhythm dependence
steps.text: In complete block the atria and ventricles are fully dissociated. The ventricles depend entirely on a subsidiary pacemaker, which may be slow, unreliable or fail altogether.

steps.title: Haemodynamic consequences
steps.text: Bradycardia reduces cardiac output once stroke volume can no longer compensate, and loss of atrioventricular synchrony reduces filling and produces cannon a waves. Long pauses cause syncope; prolonged asystole is fatal, which is why pacing is the definitive treatment.
